segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw a beast rising out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, and on its horns ten diadems, and on its heads blasphemous names.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the beast that I saw was like a leopard, and its feet were like a bear’s, and its mouth was like a lion’s mouth. And the dragon gave it his power and his throne and great authority.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And one of its heads looked as though it had been slaughtered to death, yet its mortal wound was healed. And the whole earth marveled and followed the beast,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they worshiped the dragon because he had given the authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Who is like the beast, and who can wage war against it?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And it was given a mouth speaking boastful words and blasphemies, and it was given authority to act for forty-two months.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And it opened its mouth in blasphemies against God, to blaspheme his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And it was allowed to make war on the holy ones and to conquer them, and it was given authority over every tribe and people and language and nation.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And all who live on the earth will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written in the book of life of the Lamb who was slaughtered from the foundation of the world.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone has an ear, let them hear.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone is for captivity, into captivity they go. If anyone is to be killed by the sword, by the sword they are to be killed. Here is the endurance and the faith of the holy ones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw another beast rising out of the earth, and it had two horns like a lamb, and it spoke like a dragon.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And it exercises all the authority of the first beast in its sight. And it makes the earth and those who live in it worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And it performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to the earth in the sight of people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And it deceives those who live on the earth because of the signs it was allowed to perform in the sight of the beast, telling those who live on the earth to make an image for the beast that has the wound of the sword and yet lived.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And it was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast would even speak and would cause all who do not worship the image of the beast to be killed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And it causes everyone, the small and the great, the rich and the poor, the free and the slaves, to be given a mark on their right hand or on their forehead,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that no one can buy or sell except the one who has the mark, the name of the beast or the number of its name.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Here is wisdom. Let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a person, and its number is six hundred sixty-six.

notes.note: The description draws on Daniel 7, where four beasts rise from the sea in turn: one like a lion, one like a bear, one like a leopard, and a fourth with ten horns. Here their features are combined in a single beast. In Daniel the beasts stand for successive empires, and a first-century reader would have heard this one as an image of imperial power.

notes.traditional: wounded to death; seemed to have a mortal wound
notes.note: Most translations soften this to “wounded.” The Greek uses the same verb, in the same form, that describes the Lamb “as though slaughtered” in 5:6 and “slaughtered” in verse 8. Rendering it the same way lets the reader see that the beast is presented as a counterfeit of the Lamb.

The same passive verb recurs through the chapter, rendered “was given” with a noun and “was allowed” with a verb (verses 7, 14, 15). No giver is named. Most interpreters take the repeated passive to mean that the beast acts only within limits set by God, though in verses 2 and 4 the dragon is the one who gives the beast its authority.

The Greek word means “tent” and recalls Israel’s tent-sanctuary in the wilderness. It is rendered “dwelling” here because the verb that follows, “dwell,” comes from the same root, and the wordplay would otherwise be lost. Some manuscripts add “and” before “those who dwell in heaven,” making them a third object; the text translated here identifies God’s dwelling with those heavenly dwellers.

The traditional “saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek term is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

The Greek verb is the ordinary word for winning a victory in battle. It is the same verb used for the promises “to the one who conquers” in chapters 2 and 3. Older versions use “overcome”; several modern versions use “conquer” in Revelation, and the meaning is not disputed.

The Greek word here is the same one translated “Gentiles” elsewhere in the New Testament. It means a people or nation, and in the plural often the non-Jewish peoples. In this fourfold list the sense is plainly all the peoples of the world.

notes.phrase: slaughtered from the foundation of the world
notes.note: The translation follows the Greek word order, in which “from the foundation of the world” stands directly after “slaughtered.” The phrase can instead be attached to “written,” giving “whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slaughtered.” The closely parallel wording of 17:8 supports that alternative. Translations and commentators are divided.

notes.phrase: If anyone is to be killed by the sword, by the sword they are to be killed
notes.note: The manuscripts differ considerably here. The text translated, which follows Codex Alexandrinus, speaks of the fate believers must accept and echoes Jeremiah 15:2. Many other manuscripts read “if anyone kills with the sword, with the sword he must be killed,” a warning of retribution, and several well-known translations follow that reading.

The Greek word means both “breath” and “spirit,” and either is possible; the point is that the image is made to seem alive. It is also unclear whether the one who causes the killing is the image or the second beast. The Greek grammar slightly favors the image.

The Greek word was used for a stamped, engraved, or branded impression, including the imprint on coins and official seals. The mark on the hand or forehead parodies the seal placed on the foreheads of God’s servants in 7:3. Whether the author had a specific practice in view is uncertain.

The phrase can mean the number of a particular individual, whose name adds up to the figure given, or simply “a human number,” one reckoned in the ordinary human way (compare 21:17). Most interpreters take it as pointing to an individual. Traditional versions have “the number of a man.”

In Greek and Hebrew, letters also served as numerals, so any name had a numerical total. The most widely held view is that the number comes from “Nero Caesar” written in Hebrew letters, though this is not certain and other solutions have been proposed. A few early manuscripts read six hundred sixteen, a variant already known in the second century; it fits a different spelling of the same name.

Translations vary among patience, perseverance, steadfastness and endurance across the letters and Revelation, and the reader should see one word.
Used of the Lamb, the beast’s head and the martyrs in Revelation; “slain,” “wounded” and “slaughtered” in different places would hide the deliberate parallel.
“Those who live on the earth” is a fixed phrase in Revelation and must be kept distinct from σκηνόω “dwell,” which the register pairs with “dwelling.”
